note: Narration for the moon-phases exemplar. In production these lines are the teacher's own turn (planner writes them as content, the voice lane speaks them); here they are synthesized once so the timeline can be built from MEASURED clause durations (teacher-stage-cue-scheduler: phrase captions, clause cues, 400 ms pre-roll).
instructions: A warm, clear Indian teacher talking to a 12-year-old in English. Conversational and a little dry, unhurried, natural pauses at full stops. Not theatrical, not sing-song.

lines.L01: Every evening, the Moon looks a little different.
lines.L02: A thin curve. Half a circle. A full disc. Then back again.
lines.L03: But the Moon itself never changes shape. So what's going on?
lines.L04: Let's go up, and look down from above the North Pole.
lines.L05: Sunlight comes in from one side.
lines.L06: The Moon makes no light of its own. The Sun lights up half of it, always the half facing the Sun.
lines.L07: As the Moon travels around the Earth, that lit half keeps facing the Sun.
lines.L08: But from Earth, we only see the half that faces us.
lines.L09: New moon. Amavasya. The lit half faces away, so we see almost nothing.
lines.L10: A few days on, a thin crescent.
lines.L11: About a week in, first quarter. We see half of the lit half.
lines.L12: Two weeks: full moon. Purnima. The whole lit half faces us.
lines.L13: Then it shrinks back the same way. One full cycle takes about twenty-nine and a half days.
lines.L14: And no, it isn't Earth's shadow.
lines.L15: Earth's shadow points away from the Sun. At first quarter the Moon is nowhere near it, and half of it is still dark.
lines.L16: The Moon slips into that shadow only now and then, at a full moon. That's a lunar eclipse.
lines.L17: Your turn. Drag the Moon to where it would look like a half moon in the evening sky.
lines.L19: Now make it a full moon.
lines.L21: That's a half moon too, but a morning one. Try the other side.
